clue.text: Heroine portrayed as a lady, or toxophilite

definitions.text: Heroine portrayed as a lady, or toxophilite

parts.words: Heroine portrayed as a lady, or toxophilite
parts.note: points to the heroine of Henry James's The Portrait of a Lady, whose surname is a word for a toxophilite, one who shoots with a bow

explanation.surface: A heroine painted as a refined lady, or else as a keen bowman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Portrayed as a lady' alludes to The Portrait of a Lady; 'toxophilite' means archer, which is the heroine's surname, Isabel Archer.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabel Archer is the central figure of James's novel The Portrait of a Lady.

clue.text: Composer in abandoned shop, right at end

indicators.note: at end places the next piece after the scrambled letters
abandoned means wild and unrestrained, so the letters of the shop are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A musician found in a deserted shop, standing at the far end on the right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandoned' reads as deserted, but signals an anagram of SHOP, giving SPOH; 'at end' puts R after it. Louis Spohr was a German composer and violinist.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis Spohr was a German Romantic composer and violinist.

clue.text: Patient and courageous little woman

parts.note: describes the gentle, brave sister in Louisa May Alcott's Little Women

explanation.surface: Praise for a small woman who is brave and long-suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little woman' alludes to Alcott's Little Women; the patient, courageous sister is Beth, of the March family.
explanation.definitionFit: Beth is the quiet, self-sacrificing March sister in Alcott's novel Little Women.

clue.text: Small character from Steinbeck? Hardly

parts.note: Of Mice and Men's huge, strong farmhand whose surname is Small, though he is anything but small

explanation.surface: A question whether a Steinbeck figure is little, answered with a dismissive no.
explanation.walkthrough: The giant farmhand in Of Mice and Men is Lennie Small; 'Hardly' says the surname belies his great size.
explanation.definitionFit: Lennie Small is the huge, simple-minded farmhand in Steinbeck's Of Mice and Men.

clue.text: Agnes, who went far with Forster

definitions.text: Agnes, who went far with Forster

parts.words: Agnes, who went far with Forster
parts.note: names Agnes, a character in E. M. Forster's The Longest Journey, with 'went far' pointing to that novel's title

explanation.surface: A woman called Agnes who travelled a long way in the novelist's company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'went far' alludes to The Longest Journey, in which Agnes Pembroke marries Rickie Elliot.
explanation.definitionFit: Agnes Pembroke is Rickie's wife in Forster's novel The Longest Journey.

clue.text: Persistently profligate, puncturing pride, personification of the picaresque

definitions.text: Persistently profligate, puncturing pride, personification of the picaresque

parts.words: Persistently profligate, puncturing pride, personification of the picaresque
parts.note: alliterative description of Smollett's roguish wandering hero, whose novel is a classic of the picaresque

explanation.surface: A string of p-words describing a dissolute rogue who deflates vanity.
explanation.walkthrough: The run of alliterating P-words hints at the double P initials of Tobias Smollett's picaresque hero.
explanation.definitionFit: The Adventures of Peregrine Pickle is Smollett's picaresque novel about a dissolute, prank-playing young man.

clue.text: Chaps surround fool and French composer

indicators.note: surround tells us the word for chaps wraps itself round the word for fool

parts.note: chaps are men
an ass is a fool
et is the French word for and

explanation.surface: A group of men gather round a buffoon and a French musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surround' puts ASS inside MEN, giving MASSEN; ET is French for 'and'. Jules Massenet wrote the opera Manon.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Massenet was a nineteenth-century French composer of operas such as Manon and Werther.

clue.text: Ardent youth has computer memory, ex officio

parts.note: ROM is read-only memory in a computer
EO is the abbreviation of ex officio

explanation.surface: A passionate young man owns a computer chip by virtue of his office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ardent youth' is Shakespeare's young lover; EO is the standard abbreviation for ex officio.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Romeo is the archetype of the passionate young lover.

clue.text: Account of love game in Indian doubles match

definitions.text: Account of love game in Indian doubles match

parts.words: Account of love game in Indian doubles match
parts.note: a sporting description of an ancient Indian treatise on love, with 'doubles match' hinting at a couple pairing up

explanation.surface: A report of a tennis game won to love in an Indian doubles fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'love game' and 'doubles match' sound like tennis, but describe the Sanskrit text on lovemaking between couples.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kama Sutra is an ancient Sanskrit treatise on love and sexual behaviour.

clue.text: King of Norway may be a first-born

indicators.note: 'may be' says the letters of the phrase could be rearranged into the name, so they are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A Norwegian king might well be an eldest son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' rearranges the ten letters of A FIRST-BORN. In Hamlet the Norwegian prince arrives at the end to take the Danish crown.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hamlet the young Norwegian prince succeeds his father's line and rules Norway's forces, claiming Denmark at the close.

clue.text: Notes of Bohemian girl

parts.note: mi is a note of the sol-fa scale, taken twice
mi is a note of the sol-fa scale, taken twice

explanation.surface: Musical notes belonging to a gypsy maiden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bohemian girl' suggests Balfe's opera, but means the heroine of Puccini's La Bohème.
explanation.definitionFit: Mimi is the seamstress heroine of Puccini's La Bohème, set among Parisian bohemians.

clue.text: Super way W. H. Davies proceeded

definitions.text: Super way W. H. Davies proceeded

parts.words: Super way W. H. Davies proceeded
parts.note: alludes to The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp, the Welsh poet's account of life on the road

explanation.surface: Praise for the excellent route a Welsh poet took.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Super' reads as excellent, but points to Davies's book The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp.
explanation.definitionFit: Davies travelled across America and Britain as a vagrant on foot, as told in his autobiography.

clue.text: Constantia Durham and Clara Middleton identified one in time

definitions.text: Constantia Durham and Clara Middleton identified one in time

parts.words: Constantia Durham and Clara Middleton identified one in time
parts.note: both women in Meredith's novel see through the self-centred Sir Willoughby Patterne before marrying him

explanation.surface: Two women spotted a certain type of man before it was too late.
explanation.walkthrough: Both women are engaged to Sir Willoughby Patterne in Meredith's The Egoist and break free once they recognise his self-absorption.
explanation.definitionFit: Meredith's novel The Egoist centres on the self-obsessed Sir Willoughby, whom both fiancées escape.

clue.text: Spring incitement, like fame

parts.note: a goad to action, recalling Milton's line in Lycidas that fame is a goad to noble minds

explanation.surface: A seasonal urge that, like celebrity, drives one on.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's Lycidas says 'Fame is the spur that the clear spirit doth raise'; 'Spring' reads as the season but means to urge on.
explanation.definitionFit: A spur is a goad or stimulus, and Milton calls fame one in Lycidas.

clue.text: Like Margaret Oliphant's curate not preferred (though later seen in charge)?

definitions.text: Like Margaret Oliphant's curate not preferred (though later seen in charge)?

parts.words: Like Margaret Oliphant's curate not preferred (though later seen in charge)
parts.note: alludes to Oliphant's Chronicles of Carlingford novel about a curate who seems never to gain preferment, though he is finally given a living

explanation.surface: A clergyman in a Victorian novel passed over for promotion, yet eventually put in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliphant's novel is The Perpetual Curate: Frank Wentworth seems destined never to be promoted, though he finally gets a parish.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliphant's Frank Wentworth is The Perpetual Curate, an assistant cleric never promoted for most of the book.

clue.text: "A poet is the most unpoetical thing in existence, because he has no — " (Keats)

definitions.text: "A poet is the most unpoetical thing in existence, because he has no — " (Keats)

parts.words: "A poet is the most unpoetical thing in existence, because he has no — " (Keats)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Keats's letter to Richard Woodhouse on the chameleon poet

explanation.surface: Keats's remark that a poet lacks a fixed self.
explanation.walkthrough: From Keats's letter of October 1818: the poet has no self of his own and is forever filling some other body.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats argued that the poet lacks any fixed sense of self, taking on the character of others.

clue.text: All Virginia Woolf's homes should have been at least this

definitions.text: All Virginia Woolf's homes should have been at least this

parts.words: All Virginia Woolf's homes should have been at least this
parts.note: alludes to Woolf's essay A Room of One's Own: a home with a room for her and one for anyone else needs a pair of rooms

explanation.surface: A thought on the minimum size of every house the novelist lived in.
explanation.walkthrough: Woolf argued in A Room of One's Own that a woman writer needs a room of her own; with someone else in the house, that means at least a pair.
explanation.definitionFit: A dwelling with a pair of rooms leaves one free as the writer's private space.

clue.text: Gudrun and Ursula were in love

definitions.text: Gudrun and Ursula were in love

parts.words: Gudrun and Ursula were in love
parts.note: names the sisters of D. H. Lawrence's Women in Love, with 'in love' pointing to that title

explanation.surface: Two women were both smitten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'were in love' alludes to Women in Love, whose heroines are the sisters Gudrun and Ursula Brangwen.
explanation.definitionFit: Brangwen is the family surname of the sisters in Lawrence's The Rainbow and Women in Love.

clue.text: Reran the new version for devout poet

indicators.note: a new version of the words means their letters are rearranged into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A broadcaster repeated a fresh adaptation of a religious writer's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new version' rearranges the eight letters of RERAN THE. Thomas Traherne was a seventeenth-century religious poet and mystic.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Traherne was a seventeenth-century clergyman and metaphysical poet of deep piety.

clue.text: Nothing to spoil mathematician-poet

parts.note: O, the figure zero, means nothing
to mar something is to spoil it

explanation.surface: Nothing could ruin a scholar who wrote verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Omar Khayyam, author of the Rubaiyat, was also an astronomer and mathematician.
explanation.definitionFit: Omar Khayyam was a Persian astronomer and mathematician celebrated for his quatrains.

clue.text: Keneally's young surgeon seen in chapel hampered by scepticism

indicators.note: seen in says the name can be spotted running inside the following words

explanation.surface: A young doctor in an Australian novel is held back in church by his doubts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen in' signals the run inside 'chaPEL HAMpered'; 'by scepticism' only completes the picture of the character's doubts.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelham is a young surgeon character in one of Thomas Keneally's novels.

clue.text: Composer in danger, manfully opposed

indicators.note: in tells us the name lies within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A musician in peril, bravely resisting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals the run inside 'danGER MANfully'. Sir Edward German composed the light opera Merrie England.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Edward German was an English composer of light opera, such as Merrie England.

clue.text: Donald Farfrae (as city father) sounds like horse's mother

indicators.note: sounds like tells us the answer is said the same as the phrase for a horse's mother

parts.note: a mare is a female horse, and so a foal's mother

explanation.surface: The Scotsman, as civic leader, is said to resemble a mother horse.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hardy's The Mayor of Casterbridge, Donald Farfrae eventually takes Henchard's place as the town's leading official.
explanation.definitionFit: Farfrae becomes the chief magistrate of Casterbridge, the town's civic head, later in Hardy's novel.

clue.text: Suitable setting for spine-chiller by Minette Walters

definitions.text: Suitable setting for spine-chiller by Minette Walters

parts.words: Suitable setting for spine-chiller by Minette Walters
parts.note: a chilly building fits a spine-chiller, and is the title of Walters's first crime novel

explanation.surface: A fitting location for a scary crime novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Minette Walters's debut thriller is The Ice House; a cold store suits a 'spine-chiller'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ice House, Walters's first novel, centres on a body found in an old cold-storage building.

clue.text: Sister of 25 from Lewis

parts.note: points to one of the four Pevensie children in C. S. Lewis's Narnia books, sister of the girl at 25

explanation.surface: A sibling of another clue's answer, taken from a writer's work.
explanation.walkthrough: In C. S. Lewis's Narnia books the Pevensie sisters are Susan and Lucy (25-across); 'Lewis' could suggest the Scottish island.
explanation.definitionFit: Susan Pevensie is the elder sister among the four children who enter Narnia.

clue.text: One of those with whom Macheath could have been happy

definitions.text: One of those with whom Macheath could have been happy

parts.words: One of those with whom Macheath could have been happy
parts.note: recalls Macheath's song in The Beggar's Opera, 'How happy could I be with either', about Polly and the gaoler's daughter

explanation.surface: One of the women who might have made a highwayman content.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gay's The Beggar's Opera, Macheath sings he could be happy with either Polly Peachum or Lucy Lockit.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucy Lockit, the jailer's daughter, is one of Macheath's two wives in The Beggar's Opera.

clue.text: Why mistake different Winchester boy?

indicators.note: different asks for the words to be made different by rearranging their letters

explanation.surface: Asking why one confused a pupil from a famous school with someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'different' rearranges WHY MISTAKE. Winchester College was founded by William of Wykeham, so its pupils take his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Pupils of Winchester College, founded by William of Wykeham, are named after the founder.

clue.text: She supervised What Katy Did at School

definitions.text: She supervised What Katy Did at School

parts.words: She supervised What Katy Did at School
parts.note: the head of the boarding school in Susan Coolidge's sequel

explanation.surface: A woman oversaw everything a girl did in class.
explanation.walkthrough: The italicised title reads as Katy's doings, but it is Coolidge's novel, where the boarding school at Hillsover is run by Mrs Florence.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Florence is the headmistress of the Nunnery school in Coolidge's What Katy Did at School.

clue.text: Ancient quarter in holy city

definitions.meaning: the old walled district of a North African city
Islam's second most sacred city, in Saudi Arabia

explanation.surface: An old district in a sacred town.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the old Arab district of a North African town and the Saudi pilgrimage city of the Prophet's tomb.
